prize_parts.citation: For a poetry that has remade Arabic poetic language through myth, fragmentation and a sustained argument with inherited forms, together with the poetics that informs the verse.

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged: Adonis alone, with the citation anchored in the poetry. I reassessed it against the chair's questions and the round-1 exchange. The claim is about formal and linguistic achievement. Songs of Mihyar the Damascene and A Time Between Ashes and Roses, as publicly described, remake the idiom of Arabic verse through myth and fragmentation while staying in argument with the classical tradition. On the later decades, which the chair asks about, public knowledge points to the long, open-ended work Al-Kitab and to later collections as continuing the project at larger scale and in changed forms. I cannot verify from the supplied record whether they deepen it or repeat it. I put this forward as a question for closer reading, not as an established fact. The essays on tradition and modernity belong to the same project as its poetics. I would therefore credit them as the explanation of how the verse works, not as a second ground for the award. The oeuvre is long and fully formed, so it can be judged as a whole. I weigh this as literary achievement on distinctiveness of voice, formal and linguistic renewal, sustained quality and intellectual depth, not as political symbolism, reputation or the count of first choices.
statement.case_against: The reservation I take most seriously is that the prosodic, diction-level and intertextual core of the claim is what translation transmits least well. My reading rests on translations and secondary accounts. That is a real limit on confidence, and I do not think it can be argued away. A second reservation is that part of his significance is historical and critical influence on later Arabic poetry. That must be kept apart from the quality of the poems, and Sward is right that the essays cannot carry the case alone. A third is that I cannot show that the later decades match the early collections. If that cannot be shown, the case rests mainly on the early and middle work. Cărtărescu's case is the strongest competing one, and I do not exclude that it is the better recommendation if the Arabic evidence cannot be made firm.

responses.point: Olsson, as chair, asks whether the B004 citation should be anchored in the poetry alone, with the essays described as the poetics that informs it, or should name the critical work as well. He also asks what the committee does about the prosodic core being untestable in translation.
responses.response: I would anchor the citation in the poetry and name the poetics only as the thing that informs it, which is what my revised wording does. That keeps critical influence apart from the quality of the poems and keeps the credit to one body of work. On the untestable prosodic core, I would not hide it. A recommendation should state that it rests on translations and secondary scholarship, and it should invite a reader of Arabic to test the claims about prosody and allusion. I would add one correction to the record. The uneven translation coverage of the essays that Olsson mentions is a reason to keep them out of the credited core, and I take it as a caution about my own evidence. It does not show any weakness in the poems.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg argues that Cărtărescu's large narrative architecture survives partial translation loss better than prosodic and intertextual effects, and presents this as assessability under uncertainty, not greater merit. He also says a decades-old, still widening oeuvre can be assessed now on its established major works.
responses.response: I accept that distinction, and it is the best argument for his ballot. If the committee puts assessability first, it points toward Cărtărescu. I still weigh differently, because I think a language-level renewal is the more durable kind of distinctiveness. I agree with his second point, and it applies to Adonis too. Neither candidate should be deferred merely because the whole is not fully settled, and for both the central works must carry the case. My difference from him is therefore not about the facts. It is about whether to prefer the achievement that is easier to judge from the outside or the one I think greater, with the risk stated openly. I have not moved, but I hold my first choice less firmly than before. I would support B046 as a final recommendation if the Arabic evidence cannot be made firm.

responses.point: Mattson accepts that the late volumes are the real test for Cărtărescu. She says the case would narrow to virtuosity of design if emotional and moral range does not hold, and that she would then weigh Adonis or Michon more heavily.
responses.response: That conditional is a fair one, and it applies equally to Adonis. The corresponding test for him is whether the later decades discover something new, not only whether the early revolution was large. I note that she would turn to Adonis if the Cărtărescu test fails. That shows how closely the two cases mirror each other. Each depends on its late work, and in each case our access to that work is partial. I would ask the committee to apply the same test to both and not set a stricter bar for one.

responses.point: Swärd says that if the poems cannot be shown to hold up, the essays should not carry the case alone, because influence as a critic is not a literary oeuvre of the first rank.
responses.response: I agree and have now written that into the citation. The essays appear only as the poetics that informs the verse, and the credited achievement is the poetry. If the committee cannot be confident about the poems, I would not rescue the case with the essays. I would then choose another candidate over crediting critical influence as a substitute. I also take her point that the limits on access to a language-specific tradition call for careful reading. They are not a reason to discount a writer, and they apply as much to Cărtărescu's Romanian.

uncertainties: I cannot independently verify the prosodic, intertextual and linguistic claims about Adonis. They rest on translations, secondary accounts and the longlist description, and I cannot verify full corpus coverage.

Whether the later decades, including the long work Al-Kitab and later collections, deepen the project or repeat it is not settled by the supplied record. My knowledge of them is limited public knowledge.

How much weight the poetics should carry in the citation, and how far critical influence can be separated from the quality of individual poems, remain open. I have reduced the essays to a supporting role.

Whether Cărtărescu's late volumes keep their intensity and moral range, and whether his poetry changes the picture of the oeuvre, cannot be resolved from the record. I rank that case close behind Adonis.
Whether Raúl Zurita is the better third option is a thin judgement. I know his sequences and landscape-scale work only partly, and I did not test them against the other two cases.

No award (P000) remains conceivable if confidence in the Arabic evidence cannot be reached. I do not recommend it now, because the central works can be argued on literary grounds and the limits can be stated openly.
Whether a co-opted member votes in committee is undocumented. My simulated vote is a modeling assumption. This is a committee recommendation, not the Academy's decision.
statement.conflict_note: No connection to Adonis or any other shortlisted writer is apparent from the supplied profile. The documented connections are collegial and personal: election alongside Steve Sem-Sandberg in 2020, work with chair Anders Olsson, marriage to Pär Nuder, and the Permanent Secretary role, which includes announcing the laureate. None relates to a shortlisted writer. The round-1 chair summary notes that I am one of three explicit B004 supporters, that my voting status is undocumented and that my vote is a modeling assumption. I disclose this without adjudicating it. My own work in literary non-fiction is context only and not evidence of a preference.
